current_example.problem:
Complete the truth table below and use it to determine whether $P \land (P \Rightarrow \neg Q)$ is a contradiction.

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,P\Rightarrow \neg Q\,$ | $\, P\land(P\Rightarrow \neg Q) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ |  |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ |  |
current_example.worked_solution:
An expression is a contradiction if it is always false, regardless of the inputs.

By completing the final column in the truth table below, we obtain the following:

| $\,P\,$ | $\,Q\,$ | $\,P\Rightarrow \neg Q\,$ | $\, P\land(P\Rightarrow \neg Q) \,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm T$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{red}\textrm T}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |
| $\textrm F$ | $\textrm F$ | $\textrm T$ | $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm F}$ |

According to the table, $P \land (P \Rightarrow \neg Q)$ isn't always false. Therefore, it isn't a contradiction.
